synopsis: A first-person flight through the boulder-strewn debris field surrounding asteroid 4 Vesta.

shots.prompt:
A single continuous 15-second first-person flight, one unbroken take from the first frame to the last, filmed as if the camera itself is the spacecraft. From the very first frame the camera is already flying forward, and it keeps flying forward, faster and faster, for the whole shot along one smooth path into the real body described below. It opens wide on the body, lit hard from the side with the distant sun flaring at the frame edge, and as the speed builds the obstacle field closes in around the camera: objects rush past on both sides and overhead, the nearest ones blurring, fine particles streaking past the lens, objects colliding and bursting apart, the body still visible through the gaps. The flight ends plunging at full speed into the densest part of the field, the frame filled with the brightest, most overwhelming moment of the whole take. One environment, one continuous forward camera move. Sound: the flight's own sound only, a deep low rumble under the whole take that grows steadily, sharp impacts exactly when objects collide, loudest in the final moments and continuing to the very last frame. Clear frame: only space, the real body and its debris, with zero text, logos, people or vehicle parts.

The real asteroid 4 Vesta, a pale grey, battered world, fills the lower half of the frame, the giant rim of its southern Rheasilvia crater curving across it, harsh side sunlight carving black shadows into every crater. From the very first frame the camera is already gliding forward low over the surface toward a drifting cloud of ejected rock ahead. As the speed builds the rock field closes in: grey basalt fragments from pebble size to house size tumble past on both sides and overhead, fine regolith grit streaks across the lens with heavy motion blur, and boulders collide and burst into sprays of glittering gravel, while the cratered surface of Vesta keeps sliding past below through the gaps. The flight ends at full speed plunging into the thickest clump of shattered basalt, a brilliant impact flash and dense rock dust filling the whole frame. Sound: a low structural rumble, sharp cracking impacts on each collision.

first_comment: Do you think small asteroids have more debris than giant planets? 🪨
caption:
This trajectory plunges through the boulder field surrounding asteroid 4 Vesta, passing near its massive southern impact basin.

The debris environment contains angular basaltic rocks ranging from meter-wide fragments to five-kilometer ejecta blocks traveling at high orbital velocities.

NASA's Dawn spacecraft mapped the surface of Vesta in 2011, revealing a heavily cratered terrain shaped by ancient planetary collisions.

Flying through this debris field is impossible because hypervelocity kinetic impacts from dense rock fragments would shatter any hull in milliseconds.

This is a simulation, not real footage. Do you think small asteroids produce more dangerous debris than major planets?
